raw_comment:
I noticed that the lowest group was just short of $40K and the highest was about $155K.  I also noticed that the first 4 groups are about what most people would consider basic human needs and/or civil rights topics.  Finally, I noticed that the other topics are all about either mental/emotional stress/struggles or physical stress/struggles.

I wonder what the biggest challenge with travel would be for the highest income group.  I also wonder if the pressures and stresses listed were self-imposed or if they were imposed by others.  Finally, I wonder if there were any students that applied outside of the $40K - $155K range and what their topics were.

I think this relates to me and my community of students because it is helpful for everyone to be aware of the different struggles people face based on their level of income.  Over the years, it has become extremely hard for students to think outside of their own situation, so this graph would help them do that.  It may also help students realize how big of a challenge the question is asking for when they go to write their own college application essays.

The title I would give this graph is: "Life's challenges, by household income, as told by University of California applicants"

raw_comment: The first thing that I noticed, while it is subjective, is that as household income increases the college essay topics become “less serious”. What I mean by this is the difference between the topics of economic insecurity, abuse, and domestic instability falling to households with an income of 65k and under, while topics like travel, sports, and failure fall to households with an income of 125k and over. While looking at the graph, I also noticed that the vast majority of the essay topics had some form of negative connotation. I wonder what percentage of students’ essays that were surveyed for this fell into Other/Miscellaneous categories. I also noticed that the essay topics were gathered for a specific essay prompt that applicants may answer, out of many different options. I wonder how this fact affected the range of essay topics and what the data would look like if it included other prompts. Since this data was compiled for only the University of California applicants, I wonder how this same data breaks down for different schools or even by state.

The title I would give this graph, ‘The Income Between the Haves and the Haves Not’.

I notice that lower income households tend to have more abuse, death and instability than higher incomes.

I wonder why travel is a problem for people with high incomes and why mental health is high on the graph. This relates to my community cause in Hawaii almost everyone deals with financial issues and so we deal with a lot of abuse, mental instability etc because of this. My family doesn't have a high income here in Hawaii but happily there is no abuse or mental instability but the things I am dealing with is financial aid for colleges, academics and sports.

This goes the same way with the background of a person's applicant as they can be biased too because of their race, wealth and disability which is hard to make of on how you can’t make someone's personal info unbiased.

raw_comment: In this graph, I notice how students that have a household with a lower income are more prone to talk about more serious struggles like economic insecurity, abuse, and domestic instability. It is interesting to see how the higher your family's income is the less likely you are to talk about more serious personal struggles. I wonder why this happens and why this advantage in our society causes people to basically have "less issues" or at least hide more of their problems to the outside world. This relates to me and my community because I live around both wealthier neighborhoods and poorer neighborhoods. I am able to see richer and less-financially stable peoples' everyday lives and some of the struggles they experience. A title for this graph that summarizes its information would be "A Family Income's Effect on College Essays."

raw_comment: In this graph, I noticed that there is a vast difference in incomes when it comes to college essay submissions. The people with the highest income talked about travel, while the people with the lowest tended to talk about economic/material insecurity abuse. I wonder why people who have high incomes tend to talk about traveling a lot. I understand that because they have a high income that they have the money to be able to travel, but there are so many different topics out there. I also notice that the people with the lowest income talk about economic and material insecurity abuse which may be something that they and their families go through in life. The people who make similar incomes tend to talk about very different topics and I wonder why that is. College essays are normally based on real-life experiences that a person has gone through. That is what makes this graph so interesting because it shows how money can affect someone's ideas and beliefs. This relates to me because soon I will be writing my own college essay, and while I have come up with many ideas, it is very interesting to see other people who have a similar financial status to my family put their own spin on their essay. The essay topics are so different so I also wonder what made these certain students decide to write their college essay based on some of these topics. A catchy headline is "Students Take On Their Own College Essay."

raw_comment: In this graph, I noticed that the family income had an effect on the types of problems that students talked about in their college essays. For example, the household incomes with $40k-$80k talked a lot about more serious and sad problems like abuse, instability, death, and mental illness. In the households with incomes $90k and higher, the problems started to change to become more types of overwhelming pressure. For example, failure, sports, bad grades, etc. I wonder about the statistics for this graph including the number of participants, how they were selected, and many other minor details that would help to understand the purpose of the graph. This relates to me and my community because there are many people applying to colleges right now and topics like these are very prevalent in the media. I also will have to experience this situation myself one day. A possible title for this graph could be: "Can Money Really Buy Happiness?: College's students and their significant challenges"

raw_comment:
Thanks to all students who responded.   Here are some of the catchy headlines that we received:  “Household Income Is Not Their Choice, But Still Affects Students' College Voice" by Maggie of Gladeville Middle School in Mount Juliet, Tennessee; “Does Your Income Determine Who You Are as a Student? And College Admission?” by Sandra of Rhode Island; "Can You Reveal Your Income Through Your College Essay Topic?" by Statistics in Forest Ridge School of the Sacred Heart in Bellevue, Washington; and “Economic Disparity and Its Effect on College Essay Topics" by Kaylan of New York.

You can continue to post responses.  Please check back by Friday, Jan. 7 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the graph, and a Stat Nugget.

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).

View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex). 

Signing off – Sharon Hessney of Boston, who read the article’s cited journal study and learned that the college essay topics are more related to family income than even SAT and ACT scores, and Leigh Nataro of Easton, Pennsylvania, who is grateful she only had to read 400+ comments to this prompt and not 3,519 college essays.

What do I notice?
The first thing I notice is that the students with the greatest incomes talked about travel, whereas those with the lowest incomes wrote about economic/material insecurity. The lowest salary is roughly $39,000, and the highest is around $155,000, a significant disparity.

What do I wonder?
I wonder why the graph was made? I also want to know how many people wrote about each topic. 

How does this relate to you and your community?
 This is relevant to me and my community because everyone from my school goes to college. Finding a unique essay topic is difficult, especially when people in my community all live relatively similar lives. 

Headline:
“How much does family income impact college?”

The graph is of the relationship between the subject of student essays and the average household income of the students. The subject is in response to the question of what were their most difficult challenges. The subject with the lowest income is economic/material insecurity, and the subject with the highest income is travel. The lowest four subjects are some sort of hardship or difficulty in life. 

I wonder why students considered travel to be challenging, it is an odd one out because all of the other subjects are standard life challenges. I wonder why discrimination is at $100k, I would have expected it to be lower because financial discrimination is a type of discrimination. I wonder why failure is the second highest income.

This impacts me and my community because I am a high school senior. I just wrote a college essay a couple months ago, and the subject of a college essay is a very important choice.

“Do Wealthier Students Have Less Problems?”

raw_comment:
I would argue that as the average household income increases, the college essays actually become more personal. In a way, topics such as Economic/Material Insecurity, Immigration, Abuse are more about how the outside world affects them, while topics like Failure, Sports, and Relationships are more about their own actions. This could be because many students of higher income are aware of their privilege, and instead of writing about things that were given to them, they write about topics they were more personally involved in. 

I wonder about the distribution of the data, and how many essays were actually written about each subject. I also would want to know how spread out the averages are. For example, do most people who write about academics have an income of around $100k, or is it scattered all throughout the income range?

A good title would be: "The impact of money, and what that could mean for college students."

raw_comment:
One of the things that really interested me was the various demands and problems in relation to the income levels. In lower income essays, they mainly talked about immediate problems that are much more likely to happen when you are poor, like the chances of abuse, hunger, and lack of affordable housing. In middle class essays, they mainly talked about emotional difficulties, which are likely to happen if you're pressured by those around you to rise up the social ladder and become wealthier. And in wealthier families, most of their problems stem from their wealth, like maybe a problem during a vacation or a sports dispute, extras that the other families would be less likely to afford. 

One category that really stuck out to me was discrimination, and how it was firmly in the middle of the income range. I guess maybe when people of color are a part of the middle class, they are likely to live in suburbs, which might be more discrminatory to them. Or, maybe it's because if you're an ambitious woman or POC or both, you might be more likely to encounter bigots who will try to slow you down.

This isn't really answering the questions, but were observations that I made. If there isn't already a title for it, it would be "Money doesn't always buy true happiness"

raw_comment:
The graph gave me no surprises.
 
Students with a higher average household income wrote about topics such as travel, sports, relationships, and failure while students from lower-income households chose to write about financial insecurity, domestic instability, and abuse, indicating that these topics are what pose the greatest challenges to these students. This is exactly what I would expect; students who, in reality, have lower income rates than average will experience economic and material insecurity while students with higher household incomes will find challenges in their life experiences whether that be sports, relationships, or travel. The reality is that money does define where your issues may lie, and where your issues lie impacts the way you live. Whether or not money SHOULD define where your greatest obstacles will be is the real question.

This graph gave me no surprises, but it gave me a question to think about.
"The Way Money Impacts Our Lives - to be Expected"

raw_comment: One thing that I noticed about the graph was the note at the bottom which mentions how authors manually classified essays and how the incomes were self-reported, while this doesn't necessarily invalidate the data, it does mean it should all be taken with a grain of salt because the data could be wrong. Poor people tend to write their college essays about economic insecurity because they have experienced it. raw_comment:
A good headline for this graph might be: Wages and Worries.

One of my observations on this is that the graph has lower income families dealing with serious topics, while families with higher incomes deal with less serious topics. One thing I noticed, however, is that the graph doesn't necessarily cover all the incomes. Most of this graph would be working class families, but even on the higher end, that might still only be considered middle class.

I do wonder if there was a reason for choosing the selected categories on this topic for the graph.

This does relate to me and my community due to the fact that everyone in my community has different wages, and each person has their own sets of problems. That, however, doesn't mean people from low or high income families can write about different topics outside of their income. Take for example: A low income family can write about sports, while a student from a high income family can write about death. Everyone in life has problems, it is just that some of those are influenced by the environment.

The more serious responses to personal challenges (economic/material insecurity, abuse, immigration, and death) tend to be from lower-income homes. I was also surprised that discrimination/stereotypes came from relatively higher-income households.

This doesn't mean that there isn't abuse in higher-income households in any way but it is a good measure to check your privilege.

raw_comment:
1) I think that the most notable aspect of this graph is the range of topics from more serious issues to essays that showcase positive experiences. I think that this graph further reflects our society at large, and accurately illustrates the hardships of living in a capitalist society and the privileges of the upper-class.

2) As a country that supposedly takes pride in its students, achievements, and academia, why do mere teenagers have to share their hardships as fairy tales, essentially entertaining the college board, to simply take the next step in pursuing knowledge of their choosing? 

3) I think this article relates to my community because many students too feel disdain for the American education system and do hope to see some change. 

4) A large reason I want to go to college is less so that I can continue to educate myself on subjects that I'm passionate about and more-so so that I can “get a degree, a good job, and have an honest income” as we are told to do so. In fact the careers I'm interested in, the majors I wish to pursue, don’t provide enough to live ideally and stably as one would like. I also don’t wish to subject myself to societal labels such as “uneducated” for choosing not to further an education that could potentially strip me of the wealth I'm told to go after.

Headline: Mom, is my college essay done?

raw_comment:
I notice:

I notice that within each topic there is either a high or a low amount of income. The students with the highest income talked more about traveling, and sports which are more like hobbies and the personal experiences the students have gone through, whereas the students with lower income talked more about really personal topics, personal challenges, maybe things that made them, them today.

I wonder:

Since economic and material insecurity is the highest one, I wonder how many students go through this challenge. Also I wonder why students with higher household income talked about failure. I understand that every student goes through peer pressure but do they feel like they have more pressure due to having more money? Pressure from their families?

Relating to myself and community:

This relates to my community and I because everyone goes through one of these personal challenges and or experiences, and I also want to go to college myself.

Headline:

Does your income determine who you are as a student? And or college admission?

Most students in the 90-100k income write about a physical challege(ex. death, mental wellness, ect.). The higher income students have less impactful topics.
I wonder: Which essay topic most often gets accepted? Does the essay topic of the student affect their financial aid? Does the severity of their topic affect their college experience? This graph gives me a wider view of the world of college admissions, and I have more knowledge about essay topics.

raw_comment:
The first thing I noticed was that the households with the highest income wrote about failure and travel. Many incomes that fall in the middle tend to be about physical and mental health, while lower incomes write about economic concerns and abuse. 

One thing I wonder is why people with higher incomes write about travel and failure. Was that their biggest challenge during their childhood years that they needed to overcome? What about the students who were struggling financially and had to help their parents by picking up a second job or taking care of relatives? More importantly, how can colleges take in proportional amounts of students of different incomes without seeming biased? 

This affects me because I will be applying to college later this year, along with my classmates. I wonder how this chart affects my own changes of getting into college.

raw_comment:
I noticed that the more modern-day subjects have higher household incomes, with travel, sports, and emotions being some of the top couple. However, subjects that might've been spoken about a couple decades ago have a lower household income, including immigration, domestic instability, and abuse.

I wonder why people with higher household incomes are writing about things you'd see on social media? Does it have to do with them also keeping up with modern-day jobs or even the stock market? And does the lower household economic students' parents stick to older jobs like office workers?

This graph relates to me because I am aiming to go to collage

raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's live moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graph shows the relationship between the college essay subjects students chose to answer the prompt “Describe the most significant challenge you have faced and the steps you have taken to overcome this challenge” and their family’s household income. Evidence was gathered in November 2016, before the pandemic, from 60,000 University of California applications.

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?”, “What do you wonder?"  and “How will this affect you?”  Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in this graph. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included thus graph and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series.
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released by Friday, Jan 7 with moderation on Wednesday, Jan. 12.  The topic – international Covid vaccination rates.  Keep noticing and wondering.

raw_comment:
I noticed as the household income increases it seems that the subject is less personal around the $100k margin. Students with low household incomes tend to write about personal issues such as domestic instability and abuse. However, those with higher household incomes write less about personal issues and instead about travels and sports. 
I wonder what people wrote about failure. Failure could be very broad and it depends on how people look at it. So for someone that has a $140k household income are their failures far different from those of low household income. 
This relates to me because now I wonder if my college essay was influenced by my household. It also relates to my community because I have realized that the divide between the high and low income households are far more different than what I anticipated. 
A headline idea could be “How could income levels affect a students college essay”

Possible title: The income essay; can the topic of a student's college essay tell you about their income?

This graph impacts my community as someone applying to college because according to this graph the essay topic of my college essay was likely influenced by my parent's income, something I have virtually no control over.

raw_comment:
From the graph, I noticed that as average reported household income of students increased, the issues they discussed in their essays became more materialistic. For example, students with lower household incomes discussed serious, personal topics like abuse, immigration, and economic insecurity, while students with higher household incomes discussed topics like sports, failure, and travel that was not related to immigration and relocation.
I wonder if students with lower average household incomes discuss mostly serious, personal issues because they were faced with lots of hardship in their lifetime due to their family's income, and are more open considering they likely experienced these hardships for most of their lives. I wonder if the students with higher average household incomes discussed more materialistic issues because they hadn't really been faced with profound, serious hardships due to their economic stability and only really knew materialistic issues in their lifetime.
This relates to me and my community because I am sure we have a wide range of average household incomes even within my school district alone, and our average household income likely impacts the issues we write about in our college essays as well. Our community is very diverse and there is a large disparity between average household incomes, and these two factors likely impact college essay topics used.
"Personal or Material? How Income Impacts College Essay Topics"

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that as incomes got higher, students tended to write about issues that corresponded with increasingly higher levels on Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs. For example, students from lower-income families struggled more with the basic-level, physiological needs, causing them to write about economic and domestic instability. Students with higher incomes, whose physiological needs were being met, tended to write about issues pertaining to their own self-actualization, such as sports and travel experiences.
2. I wonder if the topics of these essays influence colleges in accepting certain students. For example, will a college choose someone with a more concrete issue such as economic instability over someone with an essay about an experience abroad?
3. This relates to my community, as kids with different incomes and college essay topics will likely compete with each other to get accepted into the colleges of their choice.
4. Competition for College: How Family Income Influences College Essay Topics
ace_sentences: I noticed something.
As incomes got higher, students tended to write about issues.
These issues corresponded with increasingly higher levels on Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs.
Students from lower-income families struggled more with the basic-level physiological needs.

1. I notice that the higher the income presented on the graph, the less intense the topics subjectively seem to be. Topics like economic insecurity and abuse arguably are more intense to discuss than sports and traveling outside of immigration purposes. 
2. I wonder how many outliers there were that wrote about topics statistically unlikely for them to discuss in their essays. It would make sense that at least a few students found interest in topics that might not hold as significant a place in their lives, or may have topics that are significant to them that would not normally hold as much weight in the life of someone of their economic status.
3. This relates to my community because it shows the difference in essay topics that can be written about by two people of the same school. Depending on their economic position, they might write about completely different topics based on what they consider most significant to them.
4. This graph is recording the most popular essay subjects written about for college essays relative to the household incomes of students. A catchy title could be, “More Money, Less Problems”.

4.  Household Income Influencing Essays

raw_comment:
- After careful observation of the graph at hand, I noticed that lower income households dealt with harder circumstances in contrast to that of higher income households. For instance, studence with lower income households deal with economic insecurity, abuse, and domestic instability. However, students in higher-earning households write about sports, relationships, and failure. When comparing the two different forms of subject material, the lower-income households deal with harsher circumstances. 

- I wonder if students of a higher-income background understand that there are many who are simply less fortunate than them. I am not implying that their issues are not worth writing about, but rather questioning their awareness in terms of the issues of other college candidates. I also wonder if the same applies to those of lower-income backgrounds. Do they realize that students of higher-income background write about less-severe topics? This is most likely due to the fact that since they are better off, they consequently withhold less severe issues. I wonder if a study can be done to address this query. 

- This greatly relates to my community and I for a variety of reasons. I am currently an 11th grade student, and I come from a mid-income background. Additionally, I am soon going to be in the college-admissions process, along with many of my peers. It made me think about what I might write in terms of my own college essay, along with my peers. 

-The College Essay Dismay

raw_comment:
1) I noticed that the focused issue varied based on the range of average family household income. For example, relatively lower income households, including from about 40k-80k, were more inclined to write about social issues including economic insecurity and immigration. This possibly indicates a glimpse to the personal lives of these students, suggesting a possible correlation between average income and how it effects home life. 

2) I wonder what the relationship is between how much income a family receives and the likelihood of the students in the families to face prominent social issues.  I also wonder if this position almost gives lower-income students an "upper-hand" when applying to colleges because it seems as though admissions officials strive to see more "real-world" personal struggle responses when asked a prompt like this, as compared to an issue not as intense such as sports. 

3) This relates to me and my community because as a high school student I will be writing college essays one day as well. It is interesting to self asses and reflect on how my family's financial situation can effect my perspective on life. 

4)  "See Just How Much Money Effects Your Perspective On Life"

raw_comment: This graph depicts the possible correlation between a student's average family income, and the topic that they write about for their college essay. While the struggles someone endures throughout their adolescence are not dependent only on their family's income, the income plays an important role. For example, student's that wrote about economic insecurity were in families with just under $40,000 income. Whereas students who wrote about travel were in families with much higher incomes. These two scenarios make sense because someone who is in a family with a much higher income would possibly travel more because their family has the means to do so. I wonder why students choose the specific topics that they do, especially when many people have experienced numerous life-changing factors, how do they choose one? This affects me because this graph is interesting to see, especially as a Senior in high school who is in the college application process. A title for this graph would be: "How someone's life struggles relate to their family's income"

raw_comment:
Headline: Deeper Pockets, Lesser Struggles

What we notice: 
- People with lower incomes write about problems that affect their livelihood (Such as abuse and domestic instability)
- 3,000 out of 60,000 essays were analyzed 
- Higher-income essay topics were very broad
- Topics like sports and travel make sense for higher household incomes
- There is a trend line on the graph
- The wealthier the applicants got the more trivial their essay topic

What we wonder: 
- What does failure mean in this graph?
- How many essays are in each category? 
- Would results be the same if we used a larger sample size?
- Which group had the highest acceptance rate? 
- Do people with certain incomes write about similar struggles? 
- How would data change if we looked internationally?
- Do minorities write about discrimination more than other topics? 

How this graph relates to us and our community:
- Many of us will write college essays soon
- We can learn to deviate from the norm for our income
- We can learn which one is the most successful

raw_comment:
1) I noticed that college students who have written about serious challenges tend to have a lower family household income compared to college students who have written about secondary/minor challenges. For example, those who have written college essays on Economic/Material Insecurity, Abuse, and Domestic Instability ranged a family household income from approximately $40k to $65k. In contrast, sports, failure, and those who struggle with travelling (unrelated to immigration and relocation) have a household income ranging from approximately $125k to $155k.

2) I wonder if the type of university and family household income impacted the type of essay topic the college students wrote about. Is it possible for college students who have high household incomes to struggle with serious problems? How did they even pick the essays to display the following results>

3) This relates to my community because the variety of household incomes are impacted by the challenges that people face. There are a lot of reasons why someone is able to acquire and obtain the lives they have and the graph displays an example of one of them.

4) My catchy headline for this graph is: "Mo Money, Less Problems."

Something I noticed in the graph is that the greater the average income was for students, they talked about personal challenges and triumphs; They generally focused more on topics that involve a situation that revolved around situations that were mentally challenging but with less serious stakes. However, as average income decreased, they generally talked about situations where the applicant rarely had any control over their situation and scenarios that had greater real-world consequences that could seriously damage/affect the applicant or their family.

I wonder why discrimination and stereotypes are generally written by higher income students. I would have assumed that lower-income students would face more discrimination and stereotyping than richer students. I wonder what the severity of the discrimination and stereotyping the higher-income students were writing about was.

This relates to me and my community because I will be applying to colleges soon and the essay subjects many of the people in my community will be writing about will likely fall into one of these categories. All of the college essay subjects I was thinking of writing about fall into one of these categories.

What we noticed:
We noticed that as the income increases, lighter topics are discussed; students coming from lower-income houses were more likely to discuss heavier topics such as economic insecurity or abuse.

This relates to our class because we will start to write college essays soon and our community also has a wide range of incomes.

1) I notice that college applicants that come from lower income households write about topics that may be more traumatic or have had a negative impact on their lives, such as abuse and economic instability. On the other hand, college applicants coming from higher income households tend to write about topics that are less negative or may not have had a traumatic impact on a student’s life, such as travel and sports.                                                 

2) I wonder if there is any impact on one’s chances of getting into a particular college or university based on what the topic of their college essay is. Would discussion of a certain topic give certain applicants an advantage compared to the rest of the applicant pool? Would discussion of a specific topic hinder an applicant’s chances at admission to a particular college or university?             

3) This relates to me and my community, as I will soon have to write my college essay, and it is good to know what some different topics that students write about are.

4) The Far-Reaching Impact of Money: How College Essay Topics Change Based on a Student’s Economic Status

raw_comment:
What do I notice?

I notice that the lower a family’s income, the more likely a student is to discuss financial insecurity, abuse, domestic instability, and immigration in their college essays. The higher a family’s income, the more likely a student is to discuss travel, failure, sports, and emotions.

What do I wonder?

I wonder how income specifically prompts students to discuss certain topics in their college essays. For example, having low income for a family can cause stress on parents and children; never knowing if there will be food on the table can lead to abuse and poor domestic relationships if stress is not dealt with in a healthy way. Perhaps students with low domestic income have immigrants for parents and therefore have less economic opportunity than kids who have native-born parents. On the other hand, students with a higher domestic income probably had a higher education than students with a lower domestic income, as a result, there are higher expectations for those students to succeed, and they probably discuss their fear of failure on their college essays. They have the money to participate in sports and discuss their hardships/ experiences in the game. Maybe they aspire to travel which is something students with lower income couldn’t dream of.

How does this relate to me?

My community for the most part is middle class, so perhaps the hardships we discuss on our college essays will not be about money.

Title: Does Financial Insecurity Lead to Maturity?
